chunks: "Night mode is really a signal-to-noise trick.
In the dark, a tiny phone pixel only gets a handful of photons, so the picture is noisy because of photon shot noise, and no amount of clever amplification fixes that.
The only way to increase the signal-to-noise ratio is to collect more light. You can't just use one long exposure, because handheld shake and a moving subject would blur it.
So the phone takes a burst of frames, maybe 6 to 15, each exposed for a fraction of a second.
It uses the gyro to decide how long each frame can be, based on how steady you're holding it.
Then it aligns all those frames, because your hand moved a bit, and merges them, throwing out areas where something moved to avoid ghosting.
Averaging N frames improves SNR by the square root of N, so nine frames is 3 times better, which is almost 10 decibels.
After merging, the software brightens the image with local tone mapping, runs a denoiser, often a neural network, and fixes the white balance, because night scenes have mixed lighting.
OIS helps by letting each frame be longer. The trade-offs are that you need to hold still for a few seconds, moving subjects can be soft, and it costs power and compute."
